texts.preamble: A. Arikya Jarad vs The State Of Telangana And 2 Others on 8 December, 2022 Bench: A.Abhishek Reddy, Juvvadi Sridevi The Hon'Ble Sri Justice A.Abhishek Reddy And The Hon'Ble Smt Justice Juvvadi Sridevi Writ Petition No.37888 of 2022 Order:
texts.arguments: The case of the petitioner is that basing on the solitary crime registered against the alleged detenu i.e., Crime No.888 of 2022 of Medipally Police Station for the offences under Sections U/s 370, 370(A) of IPC and Sections 3, 4 and 5 of Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 (for short, 'PITA'), the respondent No.2 passed the impugned detention order, dated 23.09.2022. According to the respondent No.2, the alleged detenu is an 'Immoral Traffic Offender', as he along with his associate has been indulging in human trafficking for the sake of prostitution and running organized prostitution business with trafficked women for his pecuniary benefits in the limits of Medipally Police Station. The detenu is procuring women from Andhra Pradesh and other parts of Telangana State through his associate and enticing male customers through his known customers. Thus, he has been habitually engaging himself in unlawful acts and indulging in the acts of AAR,J & JS,J organizing prostitution clandestinely by acting as a leader/member of criminal gang for making quick money in a short period and thereby, his activities are detrimental and prejudicial to maintenance of public order. Subsequently, the impugned detention order was confirmed by the A. Arikya Jarad vs The State Of Telangana And 2 Others on 8 December, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/162210246/ 1 Government, vide G.O.Rt.No.2163, dated 17.11.2022. 4. Learned counsel for the petitioner would contend that the impugned detention order has been passed in a mechanical manner and without application of mind. Already criminal law was set into motion against the detenu. In the crime relied upon by the detaining authority, the alleged detenu was not granted bail. Thus, as on the date of passing of the impugned detention order, the alleged detenu continues to be in judicial custody. Therefore, the apprehension of the detaining authority that there is imminent possibility of the detenu indulging in similar prejudicial activities again soon after his release from jail, which would be prejudicial to the maintenance of public order, unless he is prevented from doing so by an appropriate order of detention, is highly misplaced. The alleged crime does not add up to "disturbing the public order" and it is confined within the ambit and scope of the words "law and order". Since the offences alleged are under the Indian Penal Code and the PITA Act, the detenu can certainly be tried and convicted under the AAR,J & JS,J Indian Penal Code and the said special law. Thus, there is no need for the detaining authority to invoke the draconian preventive detention law against the detenu. Hence, the impugned orders tantamount to colourable exercise of powers. The impugned orders are legally unsustainable and ultimately, prayed to allow the Writ Petition. 5. On the other hand, the learned Special Government Pleader appearing for the respondents supported the impugned orders and submitted that the alleged detenu is an 'Immoral Traffic Offender'. He along with his associate has been indulging in human trafficking for the sake of prostitution and running organized prostitution business with trafficked women for his pecuniary benefits in the limits of Medipally Police Station. Thus, he has been habitually engaging himself in unlawful acts and indulging in the acts of organizing prostitution clandestinely by acting as a leader/member of criminal gang for making quick money in a short period and thereby, his activities are detrimental and prejudicial to maintenance of public order. In the crime relied upon by the detaining authority, the two bail petitions moved by the alleged detenu were dismissed by the Court concerned. AAR,J & JS,J Thus, as on the date of passing of the impugned detention order, the alleged detenu continues to be in judicial custody and the apprehension of the detaining authority that there is imminent possibility of detenu indulging in similar prejudicial activities again soon after his release from jail is not misconceived. The crime allegedly committed by the detenu created a panic and embarrassment in the locality. The criminal activities of the detenu not only endanger the family system but also create social unrest causing widespread health hazards to the general public. Therefore, the detaining authority is legally justified in passing the impugned detention order. All the mandatory requirements were strictly followed by the detaining authority while passing the impugned detention order. The impugned orders are legally sustainable and ultimately, prayed to dismiss the Writ Petition. In catena of cases, the Hon'ble Supreme Court had clearly opined that there is a vast difference between "law and order" and "public order". The offences committed against a particular individual fall within the ambit of "law and order" and when the public at large is adversely affected by the criminal activities of a person, such activities of that person are said to disturb the public order. 8. In Ram Manohar Lohia v. State of Bihar1, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has, in fact, deprecated the invoking of the preventive law in order to tackle a law and order problem. It was observed that AIR 1966 SC 740 AAR,J & JS,J every breach of public peace and every violation of law may create a 'law and order' problem, but does not necessarily create a problem of 'public order'. 9. In Kanu Biswas v. State of West Bengal2, the Hon'ble Apex Court, while discussing the meaning of word 'public order,' held that the question whether a man has only committed a breach of 'law and order' or has acted in a manner likely to cause a disturbance of the 'public order', is a question of degree and extent of the reach of the act upon the Society. Here, it is appropriate to refer to the decision rendered by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Vijay Narain Singh v. State of Bihar3, wherein it was held that a single act or omission cannot be characterized as a habitual act because, the idea of 'habit' involves an element of persistence and a tendency to commit or repeat similar offences, which is patently not present in the instant case.
